title: Anatomy of the Ear, Nose and Throat
summary: Learn how the ear, nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx and larynx are built and connected.

lessons.title: External and Middle Ear: Tympanic Membrane and Ossicles

levels.kid:
Your ear is like a tunnel with a drum at the end. Sound is made of tiny wiggles in the air. They travel down the ear tunnel, called the **ear canal**, and hit the **eardrum**. The eardrum is a thin, stretchy skin, like the top of a real drum.

Behind the eardrum are the three smallest bones in your body. Their names mean **hammer**, **anvil** and **stirrup**. When the eardrum shakes, the tiny bones pass the shake along, one to the next, like friends passing a ball.

A small tube connects this space to the back of your nose. When your ears "pop" on a plane, that tube is opening to even out the air.
levels.hs:
The ear has three parts: outer, middle and inner. This lesson covers the first two, which collect sound and pass it inward.

The **external ear** includes the **pinna** (or auricle), the curved cartilage you can see, and the **external auditory canal**, about 2.5 cm long in adults. The outer part of the canal has glands that make **cerumen** (earwax), which traps dust and helps protect the skin.

At the end of the canal sits the **tympanic membrane** (eardrum), a thin, cone-shaped sheet about 9 mm across. Sound waves make it vibrate.

Behind it is the **middle ear**, an air-filled space holding three tiny bones called **ossicles**:
- **Malleus** (hammer), attached to the eardrum
- **Incus** (anvil), in the middle
- **Stapes** (stirrup), the smallest bone in the body, whose footplate fits into the **oval window** of the inner ear

The ossicles act as a lever and amplifier. Sound traveling from air into the fluid of the inner ear would mostly bounce off, the way your voice is hard to hear underwater. The middle ear boosts the pressure so energy gets through.

The **Eustachian tube** links the middle ear to the back of the nose. It equalizes pressure, which is why swallowing helps your ears pop. In young children this tube is short and flat, one reason **middle ear infections** (otitis media) are so common.
levels.college:
**External ear.** The auricle is elastic cartilage covered by tightly adherent skin. The external auditory canal is S-shaped: its lateral third is cartilaginous (hair follicles, ceruminous and sebaceous glands), and its medial two-thirds is bony with thin skin and no glands. Pulling the auricle up and back in adults straightens the canal for otoscopy. Sensory supply is mixed: auriculotemporal nerve (V3), great auricular nerve (C2-C3), and the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold's nerve). Arnold's nerve explains why cleaning the canal can trigger a cough.

**Tympanic membrane.** It has three layers: outer skin, middle fibrous layer and inner mucosa. It is divided into:
- **Pars tensa**: the large, taut lower part with a fibrous layer
- **Pars flaccida**: the small, floppy upper part above the lateral process of the malleus, which lacks an organized fibrous layer

On otoscopy you see the handle of the malleus ending at the **umbo** and a **cone of light** pointing anteroinferiorly (in the right ear, toward 5 o'clock).

**Middle ear (tympanic cavity).** Its walls are:
- Roof: tegmen tympani, which separates it from the middle cranial fossa
- Floor: next to the jugular bulb
- Medial wall: promontory (basal turn of the cochlea), oval and round windows, and the facial nerve canal
- Posterior wall: aditus to the mastoid antrum
- Anterior wall: Eustachian tube and carotid canal

**Ossicular chain.** The malleus, incus and stapes are linked by synovial joints. Two muscles damp loud sound: **tensor tympani** (V3) pulls on the malleus, and **stapedius** (facial nerve, CN VII) pulls on the stapes. The **chorda tympani** (taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue) crosses between the malleus and incus.

**Impedance matching.** The tympanic membrane's effective area is about 17 times the stapes footplate area, and the ossicular lever adds about 1.3-fold. Together they give a roughly 22-fold pressure gain, about 25-30 dB, which offsets the air-to-fluid mismatch.
levels.phd:
**Development.** The middle ear derives from the first pharyngeal pouch (tubotympanic recess). The external canal comes from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the tympanic membrane from the tissue between them, with contributions from all three germ layers. The malleus head and the incus body and short process come from first-arch (Meckel's) cartilage. The manubrium, long process of the incus and most of the stapes come from second-arch (Reichert's) cartilage. The stapes footplate partly derives from otic capsule mesenchyme. This explains the innervation: the tensor tympani is first-arch (V3) and the stapedius is second-arch (VII). Neural crest patterning genes, including Hoxa2 and Prx1, set arch identity, and Hoxa2 loss in mice duplicates first-arch elements.

**Middle ear mechanics.** The classic transformer model (Helmholtz, later von Békésy and Wever and Lawrence) attributes gain to the area ratio, the lever ratio and the catenary buckling of the conical membrane. Laser Doppler vibrometry has shown that the eardrum vibrates in simple modes below about 1 kHz but breaks into complex, spatially varying modes above 2-3 kHz, so the area ratio is effectively frequency dependent. Measured gain peaks around 1 kHz at roughly 20-25 dB and falls off at high frequencies. Ossicular motion also changes with frequency, shifting from pure piston-like rotation to more complex rocking.

**Round window and phase.** Sound must reach the oval window preferentially, with the round window acting as a pressure release. An intact eardrum shields the round window. If the drum and ossicles are lost, energy reaches both windows nearly in phase and partly cancels, which is the basis of the "columella effect" in surgical repair.

**Acoustic reflex.** Loud sound (about 70-90 dB above threshold) bilaterally contracts the stapedius via a pathway through the cochlear nucleus, superior olivary complex and facial motor nucleus. It mainly attenuates low frequencies, by up to about 15 dB. Its latency is too long to protect against impulse noise. Measuring it with immittance tests the integrity of CN VII and VIII.

**Mastoid and gas exchange.** The mastoid air cell system acts as a gas reservoir. Middle ear pressure depends on transmucosal gas exchange as well as Eustachian tube opening, which is driven mainly by tensor veli palatini.
levels.expert:
**Surgical landmarks.** The tympanomeatal flap is raised from the bony canal, and the **annulus** is lifted out of its groove (the tympanic sulcus). The sulcus is deficient superiorly at the **notch of Rivinus**, where the pars flaccida attaches. Posterosuperiorly, the **scutum** hides the incudostapedial joint and must often be curetted. The facial nerve's tympanic segment runs above the oval window under the cochleariform process (where the tensor tympani tendon turns). This segment is dehiscent in a substantial minority of temporal bones, often quoted as up to about 50% in histologic series, so a bulge over the stapes may be bare nerve. The chorda tympani is often stretched or sacrificed. Patients should be warned about a metallic taste afterward.

**Clinical correlations rooted in anatomy:**
- **Retraction pockets** form preferentially in the pars flaccida (attic) and posterosuperior pars tensa, the weakest regions. Keratin trapped there forms **cholesteatoma**, which erodes the scutum, the long process of the incus, the lateral semicircular canal or the tegmen.
- The **long process of the incus** has the most tenuous blood supply in the chain, so it necrotizes first in chronic otitis media. This produces a classic conductive loss of about 40-60 dB when the chain is discontinuous.
- **Otosclerosis** fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, typically starting at the fissula ante fenestram. It is treated by stapedotomy with a piston prosthesis.
- A **high-riding or dehiscent jugular bulb** or an aberrant internal carotid artery can look like a middle ear mass. Never biopsy a red retrotympanic mass before imaging.

**Diagnostics.** Tympanometry reads drum compliance: type A is normal, type B is flat (effusion or perforation, distinguished by ear canal volume), and type C is negative pressure. Wideband acoustic immittance (absorbance across 0.2-8 kHz) improves detection of effusion and ossicular fixation versus discontinuity.

**Advances and open questions.** Endoscopic ear surgery gives a view around corners (sinus tympani, facial recess) that a microscope cannot, and may reduce residual cholesteatoma. Biologic grafts and bioengineered scaffolds for the tympanic membrane are under study. A topical, nonsurgical approach to perforation repair (heparin-binding EGF in a gel) has reached human trials. How Eustachian tube dysfunction should best be measured and treated, for example with balloon dilation, remains debated.

keyPoints: Outer ear (pinna and canal) funnels sound to the tympanic membrane
Eardrum has a taut pars tensa and a floppy pars flaccida
Ossicles in order: malleus, incus, stapes (to the oval window)
Area ratio plus lever give about 22x pressure gain, overcoming the air-to-fluid mismatch
Tensor tympani (V3) and stapedius (VII) damp loud sound
Eustachian tube links middle ear to nasopharynx and equalizes pressure

test.q: Which ossicle is attached directly to the tympanic membrane?
test.explain: The handle of the malleus is embedded in the eardrum and ends at the umbo. The stapes sits in the oval window instead.

test.q: The stapes footplate fits into which opening?
test.explain: The stapes footplate sits in the oval window and transmits vibration into the inner ear fluid.

test.q: What is the main job of the middle ear's ossicular system?
choices: Matching impedance from air to fluid
Producing earwax to protect the canal
test.explain: The ossicles and eardrum boost pressure so sound energy passes from air into inner ear fluid. Converting sound to nerve signals happens in the inner ear.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the stapedius muscle?
test.explain: The stapedius is a second-arch muscle supplied by CN VII. The tensor tympani is supplied by V3.

test.q: Why are middle ear infections so common in young children?
choices: Their eardrums lack a skin layer
Their ossicles are not yet joined
Their ear canals produce no earwax
Their Eustachian tubes are short and flat
test.explain: A short, flatter Eustachian tube drains and ventilates the middle ear poorly, favoring otitis media.

test.q: The pars flaccida of the eardrum is located:
choices: Above the lateral process of the malleus
At the center, around the umbo
test.explain: The pars flaccida is the small superior region above the lateral process of the malleus. The large taut lower part is the pars tensa.

test.q: Coughing when the ear canal is cleaned is explained by stimulation of:
test.explain: The auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold's nerve) supplies part of the canal, and stimulating it can trigger a cough reflex.

test.q: The roof of the middle ear, the tegmen tympani, separates it from the:
test.explain: The tegmen tympani is a thin plate of bone between the middle ear and the middle cranial fossa. The jugular bulb lies beneath the floor.

test.q: Roughly how much pressure gain does the middle ear provide?
test.explain: An area ratio of about 17 times the lever ratio of about 1.3 gives roughly 22-fold gain, about 25-30 dB.

test.q: What is the medical name for earwax?
test.explain: Cerumen is made by glands in the outer, cartilaginous part of the canal.

test.q: The tube linking the middle ear to the back of the nose is the ___ tube.
test.explain: The Eustachian (auditory) tube equalizes middle ear pressure.

test.q: On otoscopy, the tip of the malleus handle is seen at the ___.
test.explain: The umbo is the point of the cone-shaped eardrum where the malleus handle ends; the cone of light extends from it.

kidTest.q: What is the eardrum like?
choices: A soft ball of cotton fluff
A hard, thick piece of bone
kidTest.explain: The eardrum is thin and stretchy, so it shakes when sound hits it.

kidTest.q: What are behind your eardrum?
kidTest.explain: The hammer, anvil and stirrup are the smallest bones in your body.

kidTest.q: What is sound made of?
kidTest.explain: Sound is wiggles (vibrations) moving through the air.

kidTest.q: Why do your ears pop on a plane?
choices: A tube opens to even out the air
Your eardrum breaks a little bit
Your ear bones bump each other
kidTest.explain: The tube to your nose opens and evens out the air pressure.

kidTest.q: The ear tunnel is called the ear c _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The ear canal carries sound to the eardrum.

advancedTest.q: The tensor tympani is innervated by V3 while the stapedius is innervated by VII. The best explanation is:
choices: V3 supplies muscles that act on any bone touching the tympanic membrane
They derive from the first and second pharyngeal arches respectively
The facial nerve takes over muscles that attach to inner ear structures
Each muscle is supplied by the nearest nerve trunk in the adult skull
advancedTest.explain: Arch muscles keep their arch nerve: first arch to V3 (tensor tympani) and second arch to VII (stapedius).

advancedTest.q: Laser Doppler vibrometry altered the classic transformer model by showing that:
choices: Eardrum motion breaks into complex modes, making gain frequency dependent
Middle ear gain rises steadily as sound frequency increases
The ossicular lever ratio provides most of the total pressure gain
The round window carries more sound energy than the oval window
advancedTest.explain: Above about 2-3 kHz the eardrum vibrates in complex modes, so the effective area ratio and gain fall at high frequencies.

advancedTest.q: A patient with chronic otitis media has a 50 dB conductive loss and an intact stapes. Which lesion is most likely?
choices: Thinning of the pars tensa without perforation
Erosion of the long process of the incus
Fixation of the stapes footplate in the oval window
Dehiscence of the tympanic facial nerve
advancedTest.explain: The long process of the incus has the weakest blood supply and erodes first, breaking the chain and causing a large conductive loss. Footplate fixation is typical of otosclerosis.

advancedTest.q: Why does the acoustic reflex protect poorly against a sudden gunshot?
choices: Its latency is too long for impulse noise
It mainly attenuates very high frequencies
It contracts the tensor veli palatini instead
It acts on the ear opposite the sound alone
advancedTest.explain: The reflex takes time to engage, so brief impulses reach the cochlea first. It is bilateral and mainly damps low frequencies.

lessons.title: Inner Ear: Cochlea, Hair Cells and Labyrinth

levels.kid:
Deep inside your head, behind your eardrum, is a tiny, twisty part called the **inner ear**. It is hidden in the hardest bone of your skull.

One part looks like a snail shell. It is called the **cochlea**. It is filled with liquid. When sound comes in, the liquid moves like waves in a bathtub.

Inside are thousands of **hair cells**. They have tiny bristles on top. When the waves bend the bristles, the cells send a message to your brain: "I hear something!"

Another part has three little loops, like curly straws. These help you keep your balance. They tell your brain when you spin, nod or tip your head. That is why spinning around makes you dizzy!
levels.hs:
The **inner ear** sits inside the **petrous part of the temporal bone**, the densest bone in the skull. It is called the **labyrinth** because it is a maze of connected tubes. A hard **bony labyrinth** surrounds a soft **membranous labyrinth**, and both are filled with fluid.

It has two jobs:
- **Hearing**: the **cochlea**, a snail-shaped spiral of about 2.5 turns.
- **Balance**: the **vestibular system**, made of three **semicircular canals** that sense rotation and two sacs, the **utricle** and **saccule**, that sense gravity and straight-line movement.

Sound reaches the cochlea through the **oval window**, where the stapes pushes on the fluid. The pressure wave travels along the **basilar membrane**. This membrane is tuned like a piano keyboard. The base, near the windows, responds to high pitches. The tip, called the **apex**, responds to low pitches. Because of this pattern, called **tonotopy**, different places in the cochlea code different frequencies.

Sitting on the basilar membrane is the **organ of Corti**, which holds the **hair cells**. Bending their bristles, called **stereocilia**, turns movement into electrical signals. These signals travel to the brain through **cranial nerve VIII**, the vestibulocochlear nerve.

One real example: loud noise damages hair cells at the high-frequency base first. Human hair cells do not grow back, so this hearing loss is permanent.
levels.college:
**Compartments and fluids.** The bony labyrinth contains **perilymph**, which is low in K+ and similar to extracellular fluid. The membranous labyrinth contains **endolymph**, which is unusually high in K+ (about 150 mM) and low in Na+. In cross-section the cochlea has three spaces:
- **Scala vestibuli** (perilymph), which starts at the oval window
- **Scala media**, also called the cochlear duct (endolymph)
- **Scala tympani** (perilymph), which ends at the round window

The two perilymph scalae connect at the apex through the **helicotrema**. **Reissner's membrane** separates the scala vestibuli from the scala media. The **basilar membrane** separates the scala media from the scala tympani. The **stria vascularis** on the lateral wall secretes K+ and generates the **endocochlear potential** of about +80 mV.

**Hair cells.** The organ of Corti contains one row of **inner hair cells** (about 3,500) and three rows of **outer hair cells** (about 12,000). Inner hair cells carry roughly 95% of afferent signals through type I spiral ganglion neurons. Outer hair cells act as amplifiers.

Stereocilia sit in rows of increasing height and are linked by **tip links**. When the bundle deflects toward the tallest row, the links open **mechanotransduction channels**. K+ then flows in from the endolymph and depolarizes the cell. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, and glutamate is released onto the afferent nerve.

**Vestibular labyrinth.**
- The **semicircular canals** (anterior, posterior and lateral) each have an **ampulla** containing a **crista** and a gelatinous **cupula**. They detect angular acceleration.
- The **utricle** (horizontal) and **saccule** (vertical) each have a **macula** topped by **otoconia**, which are calcium carbonate crystals. They detect linear acceleration and head tilt.
- The **kinocilium** sets each hair cell's polarity.

The cochlear and vestibular divisions of CN VIII leave through the **internal acoustic meatus**. The blood supply comes from the **labyrinthine artery**, an end artery usually arising from the AICA.
levels.phd:
**Mechanotransduction.** The hair-cell transduction channel is gated by tip links. Each tip link is a heterodimer of **cadherin-23** (upper) and **protocadherin-15** (lower). The pore-forming subunits are **TMC1 and TMC2**, supported by TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2. Deflection opens the channels within microseconds, consistent with direct mechanical gating (the gating-spring model of Hudspeth and Corey). Ca2+ entry drives fast adaptation, and myosin motors tension the links. The driving force combines the +80 mV endocochlear potential with a hair-cell resting potential of about -40 to -70 mV. This roughly 150 mV gradient explains the system's speed and sensitivity. K+ leaves basolaterally and is recycled through supporting cells via **connexin 26 (GJB2)** gap junctions. GJB2 variants are the most common cause of nonsyndromic recessive deafness.

**The cochlear amplifier.** Von Békésy described a passive traveling wave, but its tuning in dead cochleae was far too broad. Living cochleae are sharply tuned, nonlinear and about 40-60 dB more sensitive. The source is **outer hair cell electromotility** driven by **prestin (SLC26A5)**, discovered by Zheng, Dallos and colleagues in 2000. Prestin changes length with voltage and feeds energy back into the basilar membrane. Prestin-knockout mice lose about 40-60 dB of sensitivity. Hair-bundle active motility may also contribute, and how much each mechanism adds remains debated. **Otoacoustic emissions**, first recorded by Kemp in 1978, are a by-product of this amplifier.

**Synapse.** Inner hair cells use **ribbon synapses** that release vesicles continuously and precisely. Exocytosis depends on **otoferlin** and on Ca_v1.3 channels. Each inner hair cell contacts 10-30 afferent fibers that differ in spontaneous rate and threshold.

**Efferents.** The **medial olivocochlear** system innervates outer hair cells through α9/α10 nicotinic receptors. Activation causes SK-channel hyperpolarization and reduces gain. The lateral olivocochlear system modulates inner hair cell afferents.

**Vestibular hair cells.** Type I cells are enveloped by a **calyx** terminal. Type II cells receive bouton terminals. Within the maculae, hair-cell polarity reverses across the **striola**, so a single macula can encode tilt in any direction.
levels.expert:
**Hidden hearing loss.** Kujawa and Liberman (2009) showed that noise causing only a temporary threshold shift can permanently destroy up to about 50% of inner-hair-cell ribbon synapses, while hair cells and audiograms recover. The fibers most affected are low-spontaneous-rate ones, which encode sound in noise. This **cochlear synaptopathy** may explain speech-in-noise difficulty despite a normal audiogram. Its role in humans is still debated, partly because there is no validated biomarker. Candidates include ABR wave I amplitude and the middle-ear muscle reflex.

**Ototoxicity patterns.** Aminoglycosides and cisplatin damage basal outer hair cells first, producing high-frequency loss that can be tracked with DPOAEs and extended high-frequency audiometry. Aminoglycosides enter through the transduction channels. Gentamicin is relatively vestibulotoxic, which clinicians exploit in intratympanic ablation for Ménière's disease. The mitochondrial **m.1555A>G** variant greatly increases aminoglycoside susceptibility. Sodium thiosulfate is now approved to reduce cisplatin ototoxicity in children with localized solid tumors.

**Third-window physiology.** Normally only the oval and round windows let the labyrinth move. **Superior canal dehiscence** adds a third window. The result is sound- or pressure-induced vertigo (Tullio phenomenon), autophony, bone-conduction hypersensitivity, and low VEMP thresholds.

**Vascular and surgical anatomy.** Because the labyrinthine artery is an end artery, AICA infarcts can cause sudden hearing loss with vertigo. This presentation can mimic labyrinthitis, so imaging matters. In the internal acoustic meatus, the facial nerve runs anterosuperior, the cochlear nerve anteroinferior, and the vestibular nerves posterior ("7-Up, Coke down"). Bill's bar separates the facial and superior vestibular nerves, a key landmark in vestibular schwannoma surgery. Hearing preservation depends on protecting the cochlear nerve and its blood supply.

**Frontiers.** AAV gene therapy delivering **OTOF** has restored hearing in children with otoferlin deafness in 2023-2024 trials. Mammalian hair cells do not regenerate. Atoh1 activation and Wnt/Notch modulation are under study, but early regeneration trials have produced modest results. Cochlear implants bypass hair cells and stimulate spiral ganglion neurons tonotopically. They work only if those neurons survive.

keyPoints: The inner ear lies in the petrous temporal bone: a bony labyrinth around a membranous one
The cochlea codes pitch tonotopically: base for high pitches, apex for low
Endolymph is high in K+; the stria vascularis makes a +80 mV endocochlear potential
Inner hair cells send the signals; outer hair cells amplify using prestin
Semicircular canals sense rotation; the utricle and saccule sense gravity and linear motion
Tip links open TMC channels; mammalian hair cells do not regenerate

test.q: Which part of the cochlea responds best to high-frequency sounds?
test.explain: With tonotopy, the stiff, narrow base near the windows responds to high pitches. The apex, near the helicotrema, responds to low pitches.

test.q: Endolymph is unusual because it is:
test.explain: Endolymph has about 150 mM K+, so it resembles the inside of a cell. Perilymph is low in K+, like extracellular fluid.

test.q: Which structure secretes K+ and generates the endocochlear potential?
test.explain: The stria vascularis on the cochlea's lateral wall pumps K+ into the endolymph, creating a potential of about +80 mV.

test.q: Most afferent hearing signals to the brain come from:
test.explain: Inner hair cells carry about 95% of afferent signals. Outer hair cells mainly act as amplifiers.

test.q: The semicircular canals mainly detect:
test.explain: The canals sense angular acceleration. The utricle and saccule sense gravity and linear motion.

test.q: Otoconia are crystals found in the:
test.explain: Calcium carbonate otoconia sit on the maculae of the utricle and saccule, which makes those maculae sensitive to gravity.

test.q: Bending stereocilia toward the tallest row causes the hair cell to:
test.explain: Tip links pull open transduction channels, and K+ flows in from the endolymph, depolarizing the cell.

test.q: The two perilymph scalae connect at the apex through the:
test.explain: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani join at the helicotrema.

test.q: Why is noise-induced hair cell loss permanent in humans?
choices: Hair cells are replaced too fast
The cochlear nerve is cut off
Mammalian hair cells do not regrow
test.explain: Mammalian hair cells do not regenerate after they are destroyed, unlike those in birds.

test.q: Which cranial nerve (give the number) carries hearing and balance signals?
test.explain: The vestibulocochlear nerve is cranial nerve VIII.

test.q: The sensory organ for hearing sitting on the basilar membrane is the organ of ___.
test.explain: The organ of Corti holds the inner and outer hair cells.

test.q: What is the motor protein that makes outer hair cells change length?
test.explain: Prestin drives outer hair cell electromotility, which powers the cochlear amplifier.

kidTest.q: What shape is the cochlea?
kidTest.explain: The cochlea is curled up like a snail shell.

kidTest.q: What is inside the cochlea?
kidTest.explain: It is filled with liquid that moves in waves when sound comes in.

kidTest.q: What do the three little loops help you do?
kidTest.explain: The loops tell your brain when you spin or tip your head.

kidTest.q: What happens when the waves bend the bristles on hair cells?
choices: The cells make the liquid warmer
The cells send a message to the brain
kidTest.explain: Bending the bristles makes the hair cells send a hearing message to your brain.

kidTest.q: The cells with tiny bristles are called h _ _ _ cells.
kidTest.explain: Hair cells turn the movement of liquid into messages for the brain.

advancedTest.q: Why does a prestin knockout cut sensitivity by about 40-60 dB while inner hair cells stay intact?
choices: Prestin forms the pore of the hair-cell transduction channel
Prestin secretes the K+ that fills the endolymph
Inner hair cells need prestin to release their glutamate
Outer hair cells amplify motion that inner cells sense
advancedTest.explain: Outer hair cell electromotility amplifies basilar membrane motion. Without it, inner hair cells receive a weaker stimulus, even though they still transduce normally.

advancedTest.q: A patient has speech-in-noise difficulty, a normal audiogram and a reduced ABR wave I after noise exposure. The best explanation is:
choices: Loss of ribbon synapses on inner hair cells
Outer hair cell loss at the cochlear base
Failure of the stria vascularis to secrete K+
Superior canal dehiscence acting as a third window
advancedTest.explain: Cochlear synaptopathy removes afferent synapses, especially low-spontaneous-rate fibers, while thresholds stay normal. Outer hair cell loss would raise thresholds on the audiogram.

advancedTest.q: Why can gentamicin be used to treat disabling Ménière's vertigo?
advancedTest.explain: Gentamicin is relatively toxic to vestibular hair cells, so intratympanic use ablates vestibular function. Clinicians accept the risk to hearing in exchange for vertigo control.

advancedTest.q: Why is sudden hearing loss with vertigo concerning for an AICA stroke?
choices: Otoconia block AICA during an attack
AICA directly supplies the tympanic membrane
AICA runs inside the semicircular canals
The labyrinthine artery is an end artery off AICA
advancedTest.explain: The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA and has no collateral supply. Occlusion therefore infarcts both the cochlea and the vestibule, mimicking labyrinthitis.

lessons.title: Nasal Cavity, Turbinates and Paranasal Sinuses

levels.kid:
Your nose is more than two holes! Inside, it is like a cave with a wall down the middle called the **septum**. That wall splits your nose into a left side and a right side.

On the side walls are three curly shelves called **turbinates**. They spin the air around like a fan. As air swirls, it gets warmed, made damp, and cleaned. Sticky mucus traps dust, and tiny hairs sweep it away.

Around your nose are hidden air pockets in your skull called **sinuses**. They make your head lighter and help your voice sound full. When you have a cold, they can fill with mucus, and your face feels stuffy and sore.
levels.hs:
The **nasal cavity** runs from the nostrils (nares) at the front to the **choanae** at the back, where it opens into the throat. A midline wall, the **nasal septum**, divides it into two sides. The septum is made of cartilage at the front and thin bone behind it.

On each side wall sit three bony scrolls called **turbinates** (or conchae): inferior, middle and superior. Each is covered in moist lining full of blood vessels. Under each turbinate is a channel called a **meatus**, and that is where the sinuses and tear duct drain. The turbinates have three main jobs:
- **Warm** the air toward body temperature
- **Humidify** it close to fully saturated
- **Filter** particles, which stick to mucus and are swept backward by beating **cilia**

At the top of the cavity, in its roof, is the **olfactory** area, where smell nerves pass through a sieve-like bone into the brain.

The **paranasal sinuses** are air-filled spaces in four skull bones: **maxillary** (cheeks), **frontal** (forehead), **ethmoid** (between the eyes) and **sphenoid** (deep in the center of the skull). They lighten the skull and drain into the nose.

Real example: during a cold, swollen lining blocks the small sinus openings. Mucus gets trapped, causing facial pressure. That is **sinusitis**.
levels.college:
**Walls of the nasal cavity**
- **Roof**: the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, perforated by olfactory nerve (CN I) fibers.
- **Floor**: the hard palate (maxilla and palatine bones).
- **Medial wall**: the septum, made of the quadrangular cartilage in front, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and behind, and the vomer below.
- **Lateral wall**: the inferior, middle and superior turbinates, with a meatus under each.

**Drainage pathways**
- **Inferior meatus**: nasolacrimal duct, guarded by Hasner's valve.
- **Middle meatus**: frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses. They drain through the **ostiomeatal complex (OMC)**, which includes the uncinate process, the hiatus semilunaris, the ethmoid infundibulum and the ethmoid bulla.
- **Superior meatus**: posterior ethmoid cells.
- **Sphenoethmoidal recess**: sphenoid sinus.

**Mucosa**
- Most of the cavity is lined by **respiratory epithelium**: pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells.
- **Mucociliary clearance** moves a two-layer mucus blanket toward the nasopharynx.
- The turbinates contain erectile venous sinusoids under autonomic control. Sympathetic tone shrinks them, which is why alpha-agonist decongestants work.
- The **nasal cycle** alternates congestion between the two sides every few hours.

**Blood supply**
- Branches of both the external carotid (sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial) and internal carotid (anterior and posterior ethmoidal) systems.
- They meet on the anterior septum at **Kiesselbach's plexus** (Little's area), the source of about 90% of nosebleeds.

**Nerves**
- General sensation comes from V1 and V2.
- Secretomotor parasympathetic fibers travel from the facial nerve through the pterygopalatine ganglion.

**Sinus development**
- The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth.
- The sphenoid pneumatizes in childhood.
- The frontal sinus develops last, after about age 6, and is absent on one or both sides in some people.

Maxillary sinus drainage is clinically awkward. Its natural ostium sits near the top of the medial wall, so cilia must carry mucus uphill against gravity.
levels.phd:
Turbinate aerodynamics drive nasal physiology. The **nasal valve** provides most of the nasal airway resistance. It is the narrowest cross-section, bounded by the septum, the caudal upper lateral cartilage and the head of the inferior turbinate. Airflow is transitional to turbulent there, then becomes more laminar over the turbinates. This geometry maximizes mucosal contact for heat and water exchange. Computational fluid dynamics studies show that only a small fraction of inspired air reaches the olfactory cleft, and that turbinate resection alters wall shear stress and cooling patterns.

**Mucociliary clearance** depends on a periciliary sol layer whose height is regulated by CFTR-mediated chloride secretion and ENaC sodium absorption. Above it lies a gel layer of the mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B. Cilia have a 9+2 axoneme, beat at roughly 10-15 Hz in metachronal waves, and clear mucus within about 10-20 minutes. Defects explain the sinonasal disease seen in **cystic fibrosis** and in **primary ciliary dyskinesia** (Kartagener syndrome, with dynein arm mutations such as DNAH5). Nasal nitric oxide is markedly low in PCD and serves as a screening tool.

Paranasal sinus mucosa produces large amounts of NO, which is bacteriostatic and enhances ciliary beat. This links sinus function to innate immunity. The bitter taste receptor **T2R38** on sinonasal cilia detects bacterial quorum-sensing molecules and triggers NO release. In Lee and Cohen's work, T2R38 genotype correlated with susceptibility to chronic rhinosinusitis, though later replication was mixed.

The ethmoid labyrinth is the most variable region. Recognized variants include:
- **Agger nasi** cells and **frontal cells**, which shape the frontal recess (Wormald's Building Block concept; IFAC 2016 classification)
- **Haller (infraorbital) cells**, which narrow the infundibulum
- **Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cells**, which can surround the optic nerve
- **Concha bullosa**, a pneumatized middle turbinate

Why sinuses exist at all is contested. Proposals include reducing skull weight, vocal resonance, thermal insulation, crumple-zone protection and NO production. They may also simply be byproducts of facial growth.
levels.expert:
For the endoscopic sinus or skull base surgeon, anatomy is about danger zones, and CT review is a mandatory pre-operative checklist (often taught as CLOSE):
- **Cribriform plate**: Keros classification of olfactory fossa depth. Type I is 1-3 mm, type II is 4-7 mm and type III is 8-16 mm. In type III, the thin lateral lamella has the greatest risk of CSF leak. Asymmetry between sides is a recognized trap.
- **Lamina papyracea**: dehiscence or medialization risks orbital entry and orbital hematoma.
- **Onodi cells**: these can expose the optic nerve and carotid to the surgeon who believes they are in the sphenoid.
- **Sphenoid sinus**: the carotid canal and optic canal may be dehiscent in a minority of patients. Intersinus septa often insert on the carotid, so avoid twisting them.
- **Ethmoid arteries**: the anterior ethmoidal artery may hang on a mesentery below the skull base. Injury can retract the vessel into the orbit and cause a retrobulbar hematoma, a vision-threatening emergency requiring lateral canthotomy.

This anatomy is the corridor of **endoscopic endonasal skull base surgery**, important to a future neurosurgeon. Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery passes through the sphenoid rostrum to the sella, guided by the opticocarotid recesses. Extended approaches reach the clivus, planum and cribriform region. The **Hadad-Bassagasteguy nasoseptal flap**, pedicled on the posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery, dramatically reduced postoperative CSF leak rates. It must be harvested or preserved early.

The pterygopalatine fossa, reached through the posterior maxillary wall, is the key landing point for sphenopalatine artery ligation in refractory posterior epistaxis and for juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Pitfalls:
- Excessive inferior turbinate resection can cause **empty nose syndrome**, a paradoxical sensation of obstruction despite a wide airway. Current thinking attributes it to lost mucosal cooling and TRPM8 cold-receptor signaling, and conservative submucosal reduction is now favored.

Advances and open questions:
- Image-guided navigation and 3D/4K endoscopy are now routine.
- Biologics (dupilumab, mepolizumab, omalizumab) are reshaping management of type 2 chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps, raising the question of when surgery adds value.
- It remains unresolved whether "full-house" surgery versus limited ostial surgery better reduces recurrence.
- Olfactory epithelium biology is under active study after post-viral (COVID-19) anosmia.

keyPoints: The septum (cartilage, ethmoid perpendicular plate, vomer) divides the nasal cavity
Inferior, middle and superior turbinates warm, humidify and filter air
Frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain via the ostiomeatal complex in the middle meatus
Nasolacrimal duct drains to the inferior meatus; sphenoid to the sphenoethmoidal recess
Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum causes most nosebleeds
Keros type, Onodi cells and a dehiscent carotid are key surgical danger points

lessons.title: Pharynx, Tonsils and Waldeyer's Ring

levels.kid:
At the back of your mouth is a tube called the **throat**, or **pharynx**. It is like a busy hallway. Air goes down it to your lungs. Food goes down it to your tummy. A little flap helps send each one the right way.

Around the top of this hallway are guards called **tonsils**. You can see two of them if you open wide and say "ahh". They sit on each side, like lumps of soft pink pillow.

The tonsils catch germs that come in through your nose and mouth. They help your body learn which germs are bad. Together, the tonsils make a ring of guards around your throat. Sometimes they get sore and swollen when they are fighting hard.
levels.hs:
The **pharynx** is a muscular tube about 12-14 cm long. It runs from the base of the skull down to the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, where it becomes the esophagus. It is shared by the breathing and swallowing pathways and has three parts:
- **Nasopharynx**: behind the nose, above the soft palate. The **Eustachian (auditory) tubes** open here and link the throat to the middle ears.
- **Oropharynx**: behind the mouth, from the soft palate to the epiglottis. You see it when you say "ahh."
- **Laryngopharynx (hypopharynx)**: behind the larynx, leading to the esophagus.

**Tonsils** are clumps of lymphoid tissue, part of the immune system. They sample germs and help start immune responses. Four groups form a protective circle called **Waldeyer's ring**:
- **Palatine tonsils**: "the tonsils," on each side of the oropharynx.
- **Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids)**: in the roof of the nasopharynx.
- **Tubal tonsils**: near the Eustachian tube openings.
- **Lingual tonsil**: on the back of the tongue.

Real example: children often have large adenoids. These can block the nose, causing mouth breathing and snoring. They can also block the Eustachian tubes, leading to ear infections. That is why a doctor may remove the adenoids (**adenoidectomy**), sometimes along with the palatine tonsils (**tonsillectomy**).
levels.college:
**Wall structure.** From inside out, the pharyngeal wall has mucosa, a fibrous **pharyngobasilar fascia** (thickest superiorly, anchoring the pharynx to the skull base), muscle, and **buccopharyngeal fascia**. The muscles form two layers:
- **Outer circular constrictors** (superior, middle, inferior), stacked like nested cups and contracting in sequence to push the bolus down.
- **Inner longitudinal muscles**: stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus, which elevate and shorten the pharynx during swallowing.

The inferior constrictor has two parts: the thyropharyngeus and the cricopharyngeus, which acts as the **upper esophageal sphincter**. **Killian's dehiscence** is a weak triangle between them and is the site of the **Zenker's diverticulum**.

**Innervation.** The **pharyngeal plexus** carries motor fibers from the vagus (CN X) to all pharyngeal muscles except stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Sensation: nasopharynx by CN V2, oropharynx by CN IX, laryngopharynx by CN X (internal laryngeal branch). The **gag reflex** uses CN IX afferent and CN X efferent fibers.

**The palatine tonsil** sits in the tonsillar fossa between the **palatoglossal (anterior)** and **palatopharyngeal (posterior)** arches. Its bed is the superior constrictor. Features:
- Lined by stratified squamous epithelium dipping into deep **crypts** that trap antigen and debris.
- Main arterial supply: the **tonsillar branch of the facial artery**.
- Pain refers to the ear via CN IX (the tympanic branch), explaining earache after tonsillectomy.

**Adenoids** are covered by respiratory (ciliated pseudostratified) epithelium and usually shrink in adolescence. The **fossa of Rosenmüller** (pharyngeal recess), behind the torus tubarius, is a classic site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

The **piriform fossae** are recesses beside the laryngeal inlet, where swallowed fish bones often lodge.
levels.phd:
**Immunology of Waldeyer's ring.** Tonsils are **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)** but differ from Peyer's patches. They have no afferent lymphatics; antigen enters through a specialized **reticulated crypt epithelium** that contains **M cells**, intraepithelial B cells and dendritic cells. Antigen reaches germinal centers in secondary follicles. These produce mainly IgA- and IgG-switched B cells, including precursors of **polymeric IgA** plasma cells that seed upper airway glands. Tonsillar activity peaks roughly between ages 3 and 10, which matches the period of childhood hypertrophy. Tonsils are also a reservoir for **Epstein-Barr virus** (the cause of infectious mononucleosis) and a site of high-risk **HPV** infection, as crypt basal cells are exposed in the thin reticulated epithelium.

**Development.** The palatine tonsil forms from the endoderm of the **second pharyngeal pouch**; the tonsillar fossa is its remnant. Pharyngeal arch derivatives explain innervation: arch 3 (CN IX) gives stylopharyngeus, while arches 4 and 6 (CN X) give the constrictors and laryngeal muscles.

**Vascular anatomy and hemorrhage.** The tonsil receives five arteries: tonsillar branch of the facial (dominant), ascending palatine, ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and descending palatine. Venous drainage includes the **paratonsillar (external palatine) vein**, a frequent source of bleeding. The **internal carotid artery** lies about 2-2.5 cm posterolateral to the tonsil, in the parapharyngeal space.

**Fascial spaces.** Infection spreads along planes:
- **Peritonsillar space** (between capsule and superior constrictor): quinsy.
- **Parapharyngeal space**: an inverted pyramid from skull base to hyoid, holding the carotid sheath posteriorly.
- **Retropharyngeal space** (between buccopharyngeal and alar fascia): to about T1-T2.
- **Danger space** (between alar and prevertebral fascia): extends to the diaphragm, allowing spread to the mediastinum.

**Swallowing physiology.** The pharyngeal phase is a reflex coordinated by the brainstem **central pattern generator** in the nucleus tractus solitarius and nucleus ambiguus. Velopharyngeal closure, hyolaryngeal elevation, epiglottic inversion and cricopharyngeal relaxation occur within about a second. Cricopharyngeal opening is largely mechanical, driven by hyolaryngeal traction rather than relaxation alone.
levels.expert:
**Oropharyngeal cancer has changed.** HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, mostly HPV-16, arises chiefly in the palatine and lingual tonsils. It now outnumbers HPV-negative tumours in many high-income countries. These patients are often younger, with less tobacco exposure, small primaries and early cystic neck nodes. **p16 immunohistochemistry** serves as a surrogate marker. AJCC 8th edition stages HPV-positive disease separately because prognosis is much better. A cystic neck mass in an adult should prompt suspicion of oropharyngeal carcinoma rather than a branchial cyst. Occult primaries are often found by tonsillectomy or **lingual tonsillectomy** via transoral robotic surgery (TORS). De-escalation trials (for example De-ESCALaTE and RTOG 1016, where cetuximab was inferior to cisplatin) show reducing therapy is not simple. Circulating tumour HPV DNA is an emerging surveillance tool.

**Tonsillectomy practice.** Indications follow guidelines such as the AAO-HNS update (2019): obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, and recurrent throat infection meeting **Paradise criteria** (7 episodes in a year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years). Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage is primary (within 24 hours) or secondary (typically days 5-10, as the eschar separates). Intracapsular (partial) techniques reduce pain and bleeding at the cost of some regrowth.

**Deep neck infection pitfalls.** Trismus, uvular deviation and a "hot potato" voice suggest peritonsillar abscess. Parapharyngeal involvement risks carotid erosion and **Lemierre syndrome**: septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis, classically from *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, with septic lung emboli. In children, retropharyngeal abscess presents with neck stiffness or torticollis and can mimic meningitis. Lateral neck films show prevertebral soft-tissue widening.

**Surgical relevance.** Neurosurgeons use the pharynx as a corridor. Transoral and endoscopic endonasal approaches to the clivus and craniovertebral junction pass through the nasopharynx. Velopharyngeal insufficiency, CSF leak and infection are key risks. Adenoid tissue, the fossa of Rosenmüller and the torus tubarius are landmarks.

**Open questions.** Do tonsils matter in adult immune memory after removal? Large cohort studies link childhood tonsillectomy with small increases in later respiratory and allergic disease; causation is unproven.

keyPoints: The pharynx has three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx
Waldeyer's ring: palatine, pharyngeal (adenoid), tubal and lingual tonsils
Constrictor muscles push food down; cricopharyngeus is the upper esophageal sphincter
Pharyngeal muscles: mostly vagus (CN X), except stylopharyngeus (CN IX)
Palatine tonsil: crypts, facial artery supply, ear pain referred via CN IX
Deep neck spaces explain spread of infection; HPV drives modern tonsil cancer

lessons.title: Larynx, Vocal Folds and the Laryngeal Nerves

levels.kid:
Put your fingers gently on the front of your neck and hum. Feel the buzz? That is your **voice box**, called the **larynx**.

Inside it are two soft bands called **vocal folds**. When you breathe, they open wide like a door so air can get in. When you talk or sing, they come together, and air from your lungs makes them shake very fast. That shaking makes sound!

The larynx has another important job. When you swallow, a little flap called the **epiglottis** helps cover your airway, so food goes down to your tummy and not into your lungs.

Tiny nerves, like electric wires from your brain, tell the vocal folds when to open and close.
levels.hs:
The **larynx** (voice box) sits in the front of the neck, on top of the **trachea** (windpipe). It has three jobs: protecting the airway, letting air through for breathing, and making sound (**phonation**).

Its frame is made of cartilages:
- **Thyroid cartilage**: the largest. Its front point is the **Adam's apple**, which grows bigger in males at puberty.
- **Cricoid cartilage**: a complete ring just below the thyroid cartilage.
- **Arytenoid cartilages**: two small pyramids that the vocal folds attach to. They pivot to open and close the folds.
- **Epiglottis**: a leaf-shaped flap that helps cover the airway during swallowing.

The **vocal folds** (vocal cords) stretch from the front of the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoids. The gap between them is the **glottis**. During breathing the folds pull apart; for speech they come together and vibrate as air passes. Tighter, thinner folds make a higher pitch.

Two branches of the **vagus nerve** (cranial nerve X) control the larynx: the **superior laryngeal nerve** and the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**. The recurrent nerve takes a long loop down into the chest and back up. Because of this route, it can be injured during thyroid surgery, causing a **hoarse voice**.
levels.college:
**Framework.** The larynx extends from roughly C3 to C6. Its unpaired cartilages are the thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis. The main paired ones are the arytenoids. The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway. The arytenoids sit on its posterior lamina at the **cricoarytenoid joints**, which allow rocking and gliding.

**Regions.**
- **Supraglottis**: epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds and **false (vestibular) folds**.
- **Glottis**: the true vocal folds and the space between them, the rima glottidis.
- **Subglottis**: below the folds to the lower border of the cricoid.

**Vocal fold structure.** The fold is layered: epithelium, the **superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space)**, the vocal ligament, and the **vocalis/thyroarytenoid muscle**. The loose superficial layer lets a mucosal wave travel over the stiffer body. This is the basis of the **body-cover model**.

**Intrinsic muscles.**
- **Posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA)**: the only abductor. It opens the glottis.
- **Lateral cricoarytenoid** and **interarytenoid**: adductors.
- **Thyroarytenoid**: shortens and adjusts tension of the fold.
- **Cricothyroid**: tilts thyroid on cricoid, lengthening and tensing the folds to raise pitch.

**Innervation (vagus).**
- **Superior laryngeal nerve**: its internal branch is sensory above the folds; its external branch is motor to the cricothyroid.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN)**: motor to all other intrinsic muscles; sensory below the folds. The left RLN hooks under the **aortic arch**, the right under the **subclavian artery**.

**Clinical anchors.** The left RLN's longer path exposes it to thoracic disease such as lung cancer or aortic aneurysm (**Ortner's syndrome**). Unilateral RLN palsy gives a breathy, weak voice. Bilateral palsy can leave the folds near the midline and cause stridor and airway obstruction.
levels.phd:
**Embryology explains the wiring.** Laryngeal cartilages and muscles derive from pharyngeal arches 4 and 6. The superior laryngeal nerve serves the 4th arch, including the cricothyroid. The recurrent laryngeal nerve serves the 6th. As the heart descends, the RLNs are dragged caudally around the persisting arch arteries. On the left this is the ductus arteriosus/aortic arch; on the right it is the subclavian, since the right 6th arch artery's distal part regresses. When the right subclavian arises aberrantly (arteria lusoria), a **non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve** occurs, in roughly 0.5-1% of people, a hazard in thyroidectomy.

**Central control.** Motor neurons lie in the **nucleus ambiguus** of the medulla. The reflex sensory input runs through the internal SLN to the **nucleus tractus solitarius**. The **laryngeal adductor reflex**, glottic closure triggered by supraglottic stimulation, is the core airway-protective arc. Its exaggerated form is **laryngospasm**.

**Phonation physics.** Phonation follows the **myoelastic-aerodynamic theory** (van den Berg, 1958). Subglottic pressure separates adducted folds, and tissue elasticity plus Bernoulli-related pressure drop close them. Self-sustained oscillation, however, depends on a phase difference between the lower and upper fold margins. Titze's analysis of the mucosal wave formalized this. The **phonation threshold pressure** rises with fold stiffness and glottal gap. Fundamental frequency rises mainly with cricothyroid-driven lengthening and tension. Typical speaking values are roughly 100-120 Hz in adult males and 200-220 Hz in females.

**Hirano's layered structure.** Hirano described the lamina propria as superficial, intermediate and deep layers. The intermediate and deep layers form the vocal ligament. Collagen and elastin density increase with depth. Children lack a mature layered ligament, which explains developmental voice differences.

**Nuance in muscle physiology.** The PCA has specialized, fatigue-resistant fiber composition. The interarytenoid often receives bilateral, overlapping innervation. Communications between SLN and RLN branches, such as the **Galen anastomosis** and the human communicating nerve, are common. They complicate the classical clean division and may explain variable palsy presentations.
levels.expert:
**Surgical neural anatomy.** During thyroidectomy the RLN is usually sought in **Beahrs' triangle**, defined by the common carotid, inferior thyroid artery and RLN, or near **Berry's ligament**, where it is most often stretched or injured. Extralaryngeal branching before entering the larynx is frequent, and the anterior branch usually carries the motor fibers. The external branch of the SLN runs near the superior thyroid pedicle. The **Cernea classification** grades its risk by relation to the superior pole. Injury here causes subtle loss of pitch range and vocal fatigue, important in singers, and is easily missed on routine laryngoscopy.

**Intraoperative nerve monitoring (IONM).** Endotracheal tube electrodes record vocalis EMG. Loss of signal on the first side in a planned total thyroidectomy prompts many surgeons to stage the contralateral side, avoiding bilateral palsy. Continuous vagal monitoring detects traction injury earlier than intermittent stimulation. Monitoring has not clearly been shown to lower permanent palsy rates in all settings.

**Assessing paralysis.** Flexible laryngoscopy shows fold position and mobility. **Videostroboscopy** reveals mucosal wave, closure and phase asymmetry. **Laryngeal EMG** helps separate denervation from cricoarytenoid joint fixation and informs prognosis. A paralyzed fold's position reflects residual and synkinetic reinnervation, not simply which nerve was cut. The old Semon and Wagner-Grossman position hypotheses are now considered unreliable.

**Management.**
- Unilateral palsy: **injection laryngoplasty** as temporary medialization, **medialization thyroplasty** (Isshiki type I), arytenoid adduction, or ansa cervicalis-to-RLN **reinnervation**, which restores tone rather than abduction.
- Bilateral palsy with airway compromise: tracheostomy, posterior cordotomy or arytenoidectomy, trading voice for airway. Selective reinnervation of the PCA, such as via phrenic nerve donors, is an active area of research.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Anterior cervical discectomy (ACDF) carries recognized RLN palsy risk, mostly from retraction. Skull base and brainstem lesions involving the nucleus ambiguus or jugular foramen, as in **Vernet syndrome** (IX, X, XI), produce dysphonia with dysphagia and aspiration. These high vagal lesions also impair supraglottic sensation and the adductor reflex.

**Open questions.** Open questions include engineered lamina propria to treat scar, functional electrical pacing of the PCA, and better prediction of spontaneous recovery after injury.

keyPoints: The larynx protects the airway, allows breathing and produces voice
Key cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (complete ring), arytenoids and epiglottis
Vocal folds have a layered body-cover structure that makes a mucosal wave
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that opens the glottis
Superior laryngeal nerve: cricothyroid and sensation above the folds; recurrent laryngeal: other muscles
The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch and is at risk in thyroid and chest disease

test.q: Which laryngeal cartilage forms a complete ring around the airway?
test.explain: The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway. The thyroid cartilage is open at the back.

test.q: Which muscle abducts (opens) the vocal folds?
test.explain: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor. The lateral cricoarytenoid and interarytenoid close the glottis.

test.q: The cricothyroid muscle mainly acts to:
choices: Fold the epiglottis over the inlet
Lengthen the folds and raise pitch
Close the gap between the arytenoids
test.explain: By tilting the thyroid cartilage on the cricoid, it stretches and tenses the folds, raising pitch.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
test.explain: The external laryngeal nerve, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, supplies the cricothyroid. The internal laryngeal nerve is sensory to the mucosa above the vocal folds. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

test.q: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath the:
test.explain: The left RLN hooks under the aortic arch. The right RLN hooks under the right subclavian artery.

test.q: Sensation of the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds is carried by the:
test.explain: The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, is sensory to the mucosa above the folds. The RLN carries sensation below them.

test.q: A patient becomes hoarse after thyroid surgery. Which nerve was most likely injured?
test.explain: The RLN runs close to the thyroid gland, and injury weakens most vocal fold movement, causing a breathy, hoarse voice.

test.q: Why can bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy be dangerous?
choices: Folds near midline can block the airway
Swallowed food is pushed into the nose
The epiglottis is pulled off the larynx
test.explain: With both folds paralyzed close to the midline, the airway narrows, causing stridor and possible obstruction.

test.q: The loose layer of the vocal fold that lets a mucosal wave travel is called:
test.explain: Reinke's space, the superficial lamina propria, is the pliable cover in the body-cover model.

test.q: What is the name for the opening between the vocal folds?
test.explain: The glottis (rima glottidis) widens for breathing and closes for voice and protection.

test.q: Both laryngeal nerves are branches of the ___ nerve, cranial nerve X.
test.explain: The superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves both arise from the vagus.

test.q: What leaf-shaped flap helps cover the laryngeal inlet during swallowing?
test.explain: The epiglottis tips over the airway entrance to help divert food into the esophagus.

kidTest.q: What is another name for the larynx?
kidTest.explain: The larynx is your voice box in your neck.

kidTest.q: What makes the sound when you talk?
kidTest.explain: Air makes the vocal folds shake very fast, and that makes sound.

kidTest.q: What do the vocal folds do when you breathe?
kidTest.explain: They open like a door so air can get to your lungs.

kidTest.q: What tells the vocal folds when to move?
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages from the brain, like wires.

kidTest.q: The flap that covers your airway when you swallow is the e _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The epiglottis helps send food to your tummy instead of your lungs.

advancedTest.q: A person has an aberrant right subclavian artery. Why does this create a thyroidectomy hazard?
choices: The left RLN then hooks under the right subclavian instead
The cricothyroid gains extra innervation from the RLN
The right RLN may be non-recurrent, running directly from the vagus
The external SLN is shifted down to the inferior thyroid pole
advancedTest.explain: Without a normal right 6th-arch derivative pulling it down, the right laryngeal nerve can run straight to the larynx, where surgeons don't expect it.

advancedTest.q: A singer has normal fold mobility on routine laryngoscopy but loss of high pitch range after thyroid surgery. The most likely lesion is:
choices: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
advancedTest.explain: The external SLN drives the cricothyroid, which tenses the folds for pitch. Its injury spares abduction and adduction, so it is easily missed.

advancedTest.q: Why is the resting position of a paralyzed vocal fold now considered unreliable for localizing the lesion?
choices: Fold position is set mainly by the cricothyroid alone
Stroboscopy distorts the apparent position of the fold
Position reflects residual and synkinetic reinnervation
Arytenoid joints fuse soon after any nerve injury
advancedTest.explain: Variable reinnervation, including synkinesis, alters fold position, so the older Semon and Wagner-Grossman rules don't hold reliably.

advancedTest.q: A brainstem lesion in the nucleus ambiguus would differ from a distal RLN injury mainly by also causing:
choices: Weakness limited to the posterior cricoarytenoid
Pharyngeal and supraglottic deficits with aspiration
Loss of the mucosal wave without weakness
advancedTest.explain: A high vagal lesion affects pharyngeal muscles, the cricothyroid and supraglottic sensory reflex arcs, causing dysphagia and aspiration beyond the RLN deficit alone.
